content: Ovarian carcinosarcoma, also referred to as malignant mixed Mullerian tumour, is an uncommon and aggressive type of gynaecological cancer, accounting for approximately 1% or less of all ovarian malignancies. At the time of diagnosis, more than 80% of patients present with disease that has spread beyond the ovary to other intra-abdominal sites. The standard initial treatment has historically involved surgical cytoreduction, followed by either chemotherapy alone or a combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Chemotherapy regimens have included agents such as cisplatin alone, or combinations involving drugs like doxorubicin, ifosfamide, dacarbazine, cyclophosphamide, and taxol, among others. However, the efficacy of these treatment protocols has been inconsistent, necessitating further investigation to determine the most effective neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy following surgery for this rare tumour type. Additionally, it is critical to address treatment-related quality of life concerns, particularly those associated with toxicity, as the overall prognosis for ovarian carcinosarcoma remains poor. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various chemotherapy and radiotherapy regimens, either as neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapies, in combination with surgery for the management of ovarian carcinosarcoma. The study also aimed to assess the outcomes of chemotherapy alone when used alongside surgical intervention. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to February 2012. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of review articles, and expert consultations were also utilized. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy, or chemotherapy alone, in women diagnosed with ovarian carcinosarcoma. In the absence of RCTs, non-randomised studies (NRS) were considered for discussion. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies based on these criteria. Despite an extensive search strategy that identified 297 unique references, no studies met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, no data were available for analysis. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to guide clinical decision-making regarding the optimal use of neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy regimens, or chemotherapy alone, for the treatment of ovarian carcinosarcoma. To address this gap, future research should ideally involve multicentre or multinational randomized controlled trials, or well-designed non-randomised studies employing multivariate analysis to account for baseline differences. Additionally, further exploration of genetic and molecular signalling pathways may enhance the understanding of this rare tumour subtype and potentially lead to improved therapeutic strategies.
